content: Rats and mice exhibit distinct habitat preferences within buildings. Norway rats are typically found in basements and lower floors, while roof rats are more commonly attracted to upper floors and attic spaces. House mice, on the other hand, can inhabit nearly any area, including cabinet drawers and spaces above drop ceilings. Homeowners can often provide valuable and specific information regarding rodent infestations, which can aid in their management. In some communities, controlling interior rodent populations may prove more challenging than managing exterior populations. To address this, the exterior inspection form (Appendix A, 1) can be adapted for interior inspections. When modifying the form, it is essential to include details such as the level or floor, room type, number of occupants, and evidence of active rodent activity (e.g., droppings, holes, gnawed materials, and rub marks). Additionally, information about rodent bites should be documented. Metrics such as the percentage of apartments in a building showing active rodent signs are useful for comparing conditions and tracking Integrated Pest Management (IPM) progress over time. Inspection teams should adhere to standardized procedures for interior inspections. For instance, in a multifamily apartment building, inspections should begin in the basement and proceed upward, inspecting apartments in numerical order, followed by the attic or crawl space, and finally the roof, if accessible. Each apartment should be entered through the main door, and the wall containing the main door, along with all items on or touching that wall, should be inspected for signs of rodents and potential entry points. The inspection should then proceed clockwise to the next wall, continuing until all walls are examined. Subsequently, the floor area, including all items on or touching the floor, should be inspected, followed by the ceiling area and any items on or touching the ceiling. Each room should be inspected in this systematic manner, and closets should be inspected in association with specific walls of a room. This standardized inspection method provides precise data on rodent locations, facilitating targeted interventions. The data also simplify the tracking of specific changes over time and provide valuable information for other inspectors. The Block Record Exterior Rodent Inspection and Sanitation Form (Appendix A, 1) is used to document information on rodent infestations and environmental deficiencies for each premises on a block. The form accommodates data for up to 10 premises, with additional forms available as needed. Inspectors should clearly label forms (e.g., 1 of 2, 2 of 2) or indicate 1 of 1 if only one page is required. Inspectors' names should be entered at the top of the form, and other items at the top should be completed by the supervisor or team leader before fieldwork begins. The block's location should be identified by listing the names of the streets forming the block in the block diagram space in the upper left portion of the form. A copy of the assignment chart should be retained in the inspector's or supervisor's office. Completed inspection forms (Appendix A, 2) should be reviewed and initialed by the inspectors. All columns of block data should be totaled and recorded on the appropriate line of the summary form (Appendix A, 4 provides a completed example). The summary form is instrumental in preparing progress reports, identifying problems, and allocating resources effectively. As inspectors proceed clockwise around a block, they should record each street address in the left column of the form. If an indoor inspection has been conducted at a specific address, the line number (1 to 10) in the No. column should be circled. Premises must be classified into one of four categories (columns 1-4): residential, commercial and residential, commercial, or vacant lot. Only one of these columns should be checked. For residential premises, a check should be placed in column 1 if the unit is a home or dwelling (defined as an enclosed space used for living purposes). This can include single-family or multifamily units. The number of dwelling units should be entered in column 7. For premises used for both commercial and residential purposes, column 2 should be checked. For premises used solely for commercial purposes (e.g., offices, churches, schools, parking lots), column 3 should be checked. Public properties, clubs, and other nonresidential properties may also be coded for record-keeping purposes. Vacant lots, defined as lots without structures, should be marked in column 4. Parking lots, however, should be designated as commercial. Columns 5 and 6 provide additional details about premises. Column 5 should be checked if the primary function of the premises involves food preparation, sale, service, or storage, including animal foods. Examples include restaurants, grocery stores, bakeries, nursing homes, hospitals, and pet stores. Both column 5 and either column 2 or 3 should be checked in such cases. Column 6 should be checked if the main building on the premises is not in use, whether temporarily vacant, permanently abandoned, or boarded up and scheduled for demolition. If more precise information is needed, symbols such as V (vacant and habitable), AO (abandoned and open), and AS (abandoned and sealed) can be used instead of a checkmark. Column 7 is used to record the number of dwelling units on the premises. A dwelling unit is defined as a room or group of rooms within a building or structure that forms a single habitable unit for living, sleeping, cooking, and eating purposes.
